For any formula φ and a consistent theory H, φ is valid on the canonical model of H if and only if φ is deducible from H.

-- First, we consider arbitrary propositions φ. We break into two directions of the equivalence, noting that we will show both directions by the same method.

  -- We need to show that H deducible implies φ, which is φ ⊢! H.
  -- For the backward direction, we assume H deducible implies φ, and we need to show that φ is valid on the canonical model.

  -- By contraposition, if there is no φ in the canonical model, then it is consistent to have ¬φ.

  -- Since φ is valid on the canonical model, it must be deducible from the theory.
  -- Thus, if ¬φ is in the canonical model, then H ⊢! ¬φ.
  -- For the backward direction, if φ is in the canonical model, then it is deducible from H.
  -- By contradiction, if H ⊢! φ, then φ is in the canonical model.

Since we have the property of the boxes $\Box\varphi$, specifically that $\Box\varphi$ implies $\varphi$, for every formula, it follows that the condition holds: if $\Box\varphi \in \Omega_1$, then $\varphi \in \Omega_2$.

Conversely, suppose that for all formulas $\varphi$, whenever $\Box\varphi$ is in $\Omega_1$, $\varphi$ is in $\Omega_2$. Assume, for contradiction, that $\Omega_1$ is a subset of $\Omega_2$. This would lead to a contradiction because it would imply that all formulas $\varphi$ in $\Omega_1$ are also in $\Omega_2$, contradicting our initial assumption that $\Omega_1$ is not a subset of $\Omega_2$. Therefore, $\Omega_1$ is not a subset of $\Omega_2$.

This bidirectional reasoning confirms the equivalence stated.
